hook.text: In 1637, one tulip bulb sold for the price of an Amsterdam mansion. Months later, tulips were worthless. Nobody saw it.

buildup.text: Bubbles form when prices reflect what the next buyer will pay, not underlying value.

discovery.text: Shiller showed that social contagion drives bubbles. Stories spread, excitement builds, and prices detach.

twist.text: Rational people can fuel irrational bubbles. If you believe others will keep buying, riding the bubble is individually.

climax.text: Bubbles end when the last buyer arrives. When no one is left to buy, the cascade reverses and prices collapse.

punchline.text: Every bubble has a last buyer. Don't be that person.

quiz.question: What drives speculative bubbles according to Shiller?
options: Perfectly rational calculation by all participants

details.summary: Speculative bubbles form when asset prices rise far above fundamental values, driven by social contagion as each buyer expects to sell to an even greater fool. The bubble pops when belief in continued price increases evaporates and everyone tries to sell simultaneously.
details.whyItMatters: From tulip mania to dot-com stocks to housing in 2008, speculative bubbles have repeatedly caused economic crises. Understanding the social psychology behind bubbles helps identify and prepare for these recurring events.
takeaways: Bubbles are sustained by social contagion and the greater fool theory
Rising prices attract new buyers whose purchases further inflate prices
Bubbles collapse suddenly when confidence shifts and selling cascades begin

faq.question: Why do smart people get caught in bubbles?
faq.answer: During bubbles, not buying feels like a loss as others profit. Social proof from successful investors validates the behavior. And rationally, even someone who knows prices are inflated can profit by buying and selling before the crash.

faq.question: Can speculative bubbles be predicted or prevented?
faq.answer: They are easier to identify in hindsight than in real time. Warning signs include extreme price-to-earnings ratios, widespread amateur participation, and media euphoria. But timing the collapse is nearly impossible because social dynamics are inherently unpredictable.
